/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.headline: Trump says he picked ‘devoted fan’ Katie Zacharia to be next press secretary
/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.excerpt: Donald Trump on Friday announced that he had picked Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary, lining up a conservative commentator he called a “devoted fan” to be his most prominent spokesperson. Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after the birth to her second child. “It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia,” the president wrote in a social media post on Truth Social. “She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump added. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia has been selected for the role. The Guardian has reached out to Zacharia for comment. Zacharia’s selection puts her at the heart of the White House’s efforts to shape the public narrative around Trump’s second term, as his approval rating falls to record lows, and his party fights to maintain control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections. Trump has asked supporters to vote like his name is on the ballot, turning the election into a referendum on his presidency amid widespread economic discontent and an unpopular war with Iran.

/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.headline: Federal judge rules against Trump DoJ’s policy of collecting state voter rolls
/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.excerpt: A federal judge ruled on Friday that the US justice department’s policy of collecting states’ unredacted voter rolls to check them against a federal immigration database is unlawful. The ruling, by the US district judge Sparkle Sooknanan, was a setback for Donald Trump, who has pushed his administration to ramp up investigations into non-citizen voting ahead of the November midterm elections, with control of Congress at stake. The department’s list maintenance policy, adopted to comply with the president’s election integrity executive order, violated privacy laws and risked disenfranchising voters, Sooknanan said. “The court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more – a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans,” Sooknanan wrote in the 78-page ruling. Sooknanan said the policy not only violated federal laws, but also that the justice department did not have the authority to enact it because Congress gave the states, not the federal government, control over the maintenance of their voter rolls. “Behind all the window dressing, the challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote,” Sooknanan wrote.
/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.trail: Judge says justice department policy of checking state voter rolls against a federal immigration database is unlawful

/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.headline: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.excerpt: Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional. Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website. Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors. In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”.

/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.headline: Democratic Senate candidate responds to anti-trans attacks pushed by Republicans
/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.excerpt: Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina, has responded to persistent efforts by Republicans to make trans athletes in women’s sports a wedge issue in the race. In a restrained direct-to-camera statement, Andrews – a pediatrician – outlined her opposition to “biological men playing in women’s sports”, as her party pushes back against Republican attacks. “I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing in women’s sports, and I don’t support and haven’t ever performed gender surgery for minors,” Andrews said in a new ad. Andrews’ video, in which she wears a white lab coat with a stethoscope around her neck, was in response to recent attacks from Donald Trump and an aggressive ad, paid for by a super political action committee (Super Pac) supporting her Republican opponent in South Carolina, Darline Graham. The ad claims Andrews “is for they/them” and frames a transgender person as predatory toward a child. Republicans are using anti-trans issues, such as keeping trans women off women’s and girls’ sports teams, to try to thwart Democrats in the upcoming midterms. Trump has pushed the issue for years. A landmark supreme court ruling earlier this year handed Trump a key “culture war” victory by upholding laws in two conservative states excluding transgender girls and women from competing in female sports.

/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.headline: What will Democrats do if they win Congress? Here are their priorities
/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian.excerpt: In August, Jamie Raskin renewed his demand that Jared Kushner hand over documents about the overlap between his informal role advising Donald Trump on foreign policy and the private equity firm he runs after an earlier request was ignored. Five of the 11 companies that Elizabeth Warren, Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden wrote to about Donald Trump’s IRS settlement – including the Trump Organization and World Liberty Financial – never answered at all. Of course, none of them had to. That all changes if Democrats win the House and Senate in November. Control of the chamber would not only give Democrats the gavels, but they would be handed bigger staffs and the power to subpoena documents and testimony – and they have been unusually candid about how they plan to use it. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked his priorities in September: the Trump family’s businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s handling of vaccines. Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee and its likely chair, calls the potential scope of the work “gargantuan”. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, has promised to “hold the crooks accountable”. Here are eight of the most consequential investigations, what Democrats have already demanded, and where they could hit a wall.

/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.headline: ‘The real deal’: Sagal Abdi-Wali’s journey from child refugee to Labour MP in former PM’s seat
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.excerpt: For Sagal Abdi-Wali, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras, being elected to replace Keir Starmer in the north London constituency is “deeply personal”, she said in her acceptance speech. The 43-year-old has lived in the area since the 1990s when, as a seven-year-old, she fled war-torn Somalia with her mother and four brothers, eventually settling in Gospel Oak in Camden, which largely falls within the constituency. Her journey from refugee to member of parliament was one which she hoped would inspire “people who look like me”, she said. “This is Camden and this is Britain.” If she represents many in the diverse and youthful neighbourhood, however, Abdi-Wali is also very much a Labour party insider. Decades of volunteering in the community dovetailed with many years of active local party politics, even before she was elected to the borough council in 2022. She became the Labour cabinet member responsible for housing two years later, and in May was elected the first Black female leader of Camden council. She also chaired the local constituency party for four years. Those deep party and community roots help explain how Abdi-Wali was selected from a long list of more than 100 to fight the seat for Labour after Starmer’s resignation last month, say friends – and were also key in seeing off the challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. “She genuinely is deeply rooted in so many different parts of the constituency,” says a close friend who was involved in her campaign.
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.trail: Decades of volunteering combined with years of active local party politics propels Abdi-Wali to victory over Green leader Zack Polanski

/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.headline: Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.excerpt: Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will reassure Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics. The byelection, called after the former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Polanski. Abdi-Wali received 12,292 votes, 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 8,928, 33% of the vote. Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4 percentage points down from the 2024 general election. In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called. “I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me. I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden and this is Britain.” Labour’s victory provides assurance for Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.trail: Victory by Sagal Abdi-Wali in north London seat will reassure Andy Burnham in high-stakes battle for left of British politics

/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.headline: Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.excerpt: Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief. For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities. Retaining a constituency formerly held by your last leader, Keir Starmer, and which has been overwhelmingly Labour since it was created in 1983, is in normal political times not that notable an achievement, but these are not normal times. A low turnout of 38.7% and Abdi-Wali’s numerically modest 3,364 majority that resulted might not appear the greatest endorsement of the government, but it is also likely to have been in part due to the widespread assumption that Labour would win. And what of the Greens, and particularly Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England and Wales, who decided to go for the high-profile seat himself? Again, it may sound curious to think he would be happy with second place, but after the most challenging week of his political life, it could have been worse.
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.trail: It may sound odd to think Zack Polanski would be happy with second place, but after his most challenging week in politics, it could have been worse

/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.headline: Friday briefing: Burnham​ passes first test as Labour heads off Green challenge
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.excerpt: Good morning. Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, heading off a challenge from the Greens and confirming prime minster Andy Burnham’s ability to consolidate vibes into votes. Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali – who is currently leader of Camden council – won 12,292 votes while her closest rival and Green party leader, Zack Polanski, received 8,928 in a byelection that was called after former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from his London seat last month. This was a comfortable win for Labour in a contest that also saw the Greens triple their vote share. The victory will probably be framed by Labour as another bound in the Burnham bounce, while a Greens spokesperson this morning insisted that Polanski winning 33% of the vote share to Abdi-Wali’s 45% “shows just how far we’ve come”. Some, of course, will be blaming that ill thought out Zionism motion for the loss. This morning’s newsletter takes you beyond the party spin lines with our correspondents who live and report in the constituency. But first the headlines. Five big stories Europe news | High school students in France again blockaded schools and marched through cities, in the tenth day of protests that have left hundreds injured. UK news | Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants that led to his arrest, which have been ruled unlawful.

/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.headline: Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat
/politics/2026/oct/09/labour-byelection-.excerpt: Polls have closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a test of whether Andy Burnham can unite Labour’s voters or whether Zack Polanski can peel off support from the party’s progressive flank. Labour is seeking to retain Keir Starmer’s former north London seat, where he won a majority of more than 11,000 votes in the 2024 general election. The byelection is seen as a measure of the political landscape under Burnham, almost three months into his premiership. It is a significant first electoral test for Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, as part of a wider battle for younger leftwing voters who became disillusioned with the party under Starmer’s leadership over issues such as housing, the climate crisis and the war in Gaza. Polanski has sought to run an energetic campaign involving thousands of activists, leaving the Green party conference early after his speech in an attempt to prove he and the Greens are a serious rival to Labour, despite the latest polling. The Greens are hoping to reproduce their byelection victory in Gorton and Denton in February where they overturned a Labour majority. However, the political landscape has shifted since then. Shortly after their byelection win in Greater Manchester, YouGov polling put the Greens on 21%, a few points ahead of Labour. But the latest YouGov survey put the Greens 16 points behind Burnham’s Labour, which was on 27%.

/politics/2026/oct/09/nigel-farage-byele.headline: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation
/politics/2026/oct/09/nigel-farage-byele.excerpt: Reform UK has cleared two of its senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation. The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules. Party sources said they intended to pursue legal action against the undercover reporting group Verbatim, whose footage led to the investigation and was broadcast by Channel 4 News. However, Labour said the report was a “whitewash” given it was undertaken by the party’s legal secretary, Adam Richardson, a barrister with a longstanding association with the party, and Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary. Labour also said it was not credible for the party to distance itself from the scandal by claiming Orr and Jukes, two of Farage’s top team, were just contractors. Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform. Jukes, 30, and Orr, 47, will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues. Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws.

/politics/2026/oct/09/nigel-farage-byele.headline: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
/politics/2026/oct/09/nigel-farage-byele.excerpt: Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency. Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

/politics/2026/oct/09/nigel-farage-byele.excerpt: Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said. Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro. “Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.” Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.

/politics/2026/oct/09/nigel-farage-byele.excerpt: Nigel Farage has been described as a “master of the conspiracy theory” by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, after he tried to link events at RAF Fairford to small boat crossings. The Reform UK leader was criticised over his reaction to the arrests of the men on Sunday, when he said he had been warning for months about “Iranian agents” coming into the UK across the Channel in small boats. “We deserve to be told the truth about the Fairford bomb plotters’ identities,” he added in his post on X on Sunday. On Monday he posted a video in which he claimed to have received intelligence that the Iranian regime was using the small boats “to get their operatives into Britain”. Less than an hour later, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said that the five suspects were all British nationals. The men – three residents of Westminster and two others from Camden and Willesden, all London boroughs – have since been released on bail while the police investigate “multiple lines of inquiry”. Nandy told the Guardian at Labour party conference on Monday that Farage was a “master of the conspiracy theory” when asked about his comments. “I think that he’s good at using the very real sentiment that a lot of people feel, of anxiety and distrust,” she added.

/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.headline: Drumcree march standoff: protesters and Orange Order both vow to stay ‘as long as it takes’
/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.excerpt: Half a mile of countryside separates Drumcree parish church and Garvaghy Road. You can walk it in 15 minutes, listening to birdsong. The protesters gathered at each end, however, speak of grievances that go back decades and centuries to explain why a dispute once thought settled has returned to torment Northern Ireland. Up on the hill at Drumcree this week, Paul, a 64-year-old Orangeman who declined to give his surname, said for too long he and his brethren had been denied the right to parade along a traditional route that would honour Protestant forefathers who fell at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690 and the Somme in 1916. “The people of Garvaghy have nothing to fear from 35 mostly elderly gentlemen. We’re not out to cause fear or offence to anybody. We just want the rule of law to be applied.” It was a shame, he said, that Garvaghy’s Catholic residents were beholden to “militant voices”. Fellow members of Portadown district Orange Lodge No 1 – once labelled the “Vatican of Orangeism” – take turns staffing a tent filled with supplies. Some wear union jack stickers. How long will they stay? “As long as it takes,” said Paul. The mood at Garvaghy Road, also bedecked with tents, was equally determined. “It’s not about 35 men walking down this road, it’s about what they represent – sectarian domination and triumphalism,” said Tomás Óg McKinney, 57. “How long will we stay? As long as it takes.

/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.headline: Drumcree talks break up without agreement on fifth day of standoff
/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.excerpt: Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”. Speaking on Thursday night after the latest talks with the Orange Order and residents of Garvaghy Road broke up, Bryant said: “I think this is the end of these conversations. We haven’t come to a settled agreement, and it’s a shame, but my door remains open.” Last Friday’s Parades Commission decision to grant the Orange Order the right to hold a procession down the nationalist Garvaghy Road plunged Northern Ireland into one of its most perilous periods since the 1998 peace deal. A legal appeal by the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition originally scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Monday to facilitate any further talks. “Obviously we’ll have to see how that plays out,” Bryant said, indicating he would not be intervening unilaterally. “I would say that the law, in the end, is the law.” Five days of talks ended in deadlock, he said, outlining the compromises on the table for the first time.

/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.headline: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant
/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.excerpt: Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three children from a Roman Catholic family – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time. It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today. Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday. Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain. Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful. The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.

Speaking to the Irish broadcaster RTÉ on Monday morning, Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party, said collapsing Stormont “solves nothing” as it would halt critical decision-making. “Too often, we have reached for these collapse mechanisms only to have to come back six months later,” she said. The leader of the Ulster Unionist party, Jon Burrows, also said he did not “want to see the executive fall”. He told the BBC: “There are people waiting for health appointments, there are people that wait too long in A&E, people that wait too long for an ambulance, there are lots of initiatives that [health] minister [Robbie] Butler and his predecessors need delivered.

/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.headline: Loyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead as almost 30-year ban overturned
/uk-news/2026/oct/09/northern-ireland-se.excerpt: A controversial loyalist parade along a nationalist street in the Northern Ireland town of Portadown is set to go ahead for the first time in nearly 30 years, after an overnight court ruling cleared it to proceed. The Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Roadis scheduled for 8am on Sunday morning, and follows a last-minute legal back-and-forth. Northern Ireland was blighted for three decades by conflict between largely Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and Protestant, pro-UK unionists, and the Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint during the late 1990s. After a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court on Saturday, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade. Smyth had urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”. But at 11.30pm on Saturday, at a sitting of the court of appeals, Lady Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan said the high court judge who granted the injunction against the march had “unfortunately erred in law”. A new application at the high court to stop the Protestant parade from passing through the Catholic area was also dismissed in the early hours of Sunday morning. The time-limited sitting beginning at 12.20am on Sunday was heard before Justice Michael Humphreys who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances of the last-minute proceedings.

/us-news/2026/oct/09/live-stream-executi.headline: Florida execution called off after DeSantis withdraws death warrant for first time
/us-news/2026/oct/09/live-stream-executi.excerpt: Ron DeSantis cancelled a planned execution in the state on Friday, days before a 74-year-old man was due to be killed by lethal injection. The move – the first time Florida’s governor has withdrawn a death warrant in his nearly eight years in office – comes just over a week after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. DeSantis, who has aggressively used the death penalty during his time as governor, signed a letter on Thursday withdrawing the death warrant for William Lee Thompson. The Republican did not give a reason for the withdrawal, which comes at a time of increased national and international scrutiny on the use of the death penalty in the US. The bay’s cliffs loom higher and higher like stone icebergs as he approaches his destination across the bay. Noah pulls his sled carefully over a seal’s breathing hole, about the circumference of a basketball. Using a custom-made winch, he lowers a submersible instrument into the sea below the ice. Noah will bring the data it collects back to his shipping container-based mobile lab and beam the data to the south, where his collaborator, research scientist Andrew Hamilton at the University of Alberta, can review it. As the climate emergency thins the ice, jumbles up the seasons and forces millennia-old Inuit cultures to adapt, Noah is part of a scientific effort that extends far beyond Grise Fiord. He says: “This science work, it’s the first step to preparing.” The data Noah is collecting will help Hamilton and Noah understand changes taking place in Jones Sound, which empties into Baffin Bay to the east. There, in the bay’s northern reaches, one of the Arctic’s most important ecosystems is in the midst of a political and environmental upheaval – and Noah, Hamilton and a coalition of scientists have plans to better understand the changing waters before they’re beyond recognition.

Beach safety patrols in the state have reported hundreds of daily stings as the jellyfish have increased with intensifying environmental factors, including warmer waters, hot and dry conditions, and water circulation favorable to the invertebrates. Jellyfish have been spotted in the water and washed ashore across popular beach destinations, including South Bethany Beach, Rehoboth Beach, Dewey Beach and Lewes Beach, and the frequency of stings has alarmed beachlovers. Nico Caceres, the Rehoboth Beach patrol captain said in an interview: “The jellyfish for the past couple weeks have been very plentiful … The type of stings we’re seeing this summer, we haven’t really seen in past summers.” Caceres, who has been stung “plenty of times” himself, explained that the effect of stings he has typically seen in past seasons last between 30 and 45 minutes, but that this summer’s stings have caused pain and other symptoms lasting an entire day. “We have been seeing a lot of smaller children who actually end up vomiting a lot,” Caceres said. Along with many beachgoers, the lifeguards on his team who have also been stung have been avoiding going into the water out of concern about being stung again.

/environment/2026/oct/10/climate-crisis-.headline: ‘Our new normal’: how marine heatwaves affect life in British seas
/environment/2026/oct/10/climate-crisis-.excerpt: ‘It sounds silly but I thought it was a person in the water waving,” says Kurt Lander, skipper of the Yellowfin charter boat, based out of Brighton. But when he grabbed his binoculars, he realised the fluttering movement he had noticed in the middle of the Channel shipping lane was a pair of sunfish. The huge fish were lying on their sides and flapping their fins. “Apparently, they do it as a visual attraction to birds,” he says. “They’re trying to get the birds to eat the parasites off them.” Lander has seen the huge fish with their unusual round bodies before. But the difference is that those that he spotted this year are part of a surge in sightings of the species off British shores this summer, probably as a result of a marine heatwave. Marine heatwaves usually follow long hot spells on land as seas also warm. Last year was labelled “exceptional” by the Met Office, with some parts of British waters seeing heatwave conditions for three-quarters of the year, and 2026 is already showing more of the same. The extraordinary temperatures are causing shifts in marine life far beyond an increase in sunfish. Some species are moving away from warmer waters, other “invaders” are appearing for the first time around Britain’s coastline, while some marine life is dying off under the rays of the sun. Lander notices the change in the species of fish he now lands. “I used to catch at least a couple of hundred cod a year,” he says. Now, bringing in cod is rare.
/environment/2026/oct/10/climate-crisis-.trail: As warming seas push native species to cooler waters farther north, once-rare visitors have become more common
